text: On April 28, 2026, the European Parliament voted on the Yes-means-yes, the idea that RAPE should be defined based on the absence of consent, and the internet immediately got confused. In the last video, I explained that no, it doesn't mean that the law was already passed and now applies across Europe. Now let's talk about the next confusion. Wasn't Yes-means-yes already the law? What does Yes-means-yes even mean? And do we now need to sign a document before every intercourse? So, wasn't Yes-means-yes already a law? Well, not exactly. Out of 27 EU countries, around 17 already have some form of consent-based law. Inside that group, some are closer to Yes-means-yes, while others are more like No-means-no or mixed models. The remaining countries still rely more heavily on force, threats, coercion, or inability to resist. So the point of the EU debate is not that nobody had consent laws before, it is that Europe still does not have one common standard. I know it is confusing, so let me give you an analogy. Imagine that EU is a big apartment building with 27 apartments. Each apartment has its own rule about entering someone's room. In some apartments, the rule is, you can enter only if the person clearly allows you in. That is the Yes-means-yes model. In other apartments, the rule is, you cannot enter if the person clearly tells you not to. That is closer to the No-means-no model. And in older force-based systems, the rule is more like, it counts as a serious violation mainly if you broke the door, threatened them, physically pushed your way in or entered when they couldn't stop you. Still confusing? Still thinking? But how does this actually help? Well, it helps because it changes what the law focuses on. Under an older force-based model, a woman might have to show that there was force, threat, violence, or that she physically could not resist. Under a No-means-no model, the focus is more on whether she clearly refused. But under Yes-means-yes, the focus shifts whether there was clear, voluntary consent in the first place. Now, a very important point to understand is that Yes-means-yes does not cancel the presumption of innocence. Or in other words, a person is still innocent until proven guilty. The burden of proof is still on the state. It still has to prove that sexual activity happened, that there was no valid consent, and that the accused knew or should have understood that there was no consent, depending on the exact law of the country. So the legal change is not, now the accused has to prove innocence. The legal change is, courts are no longer only asking whether there was violence or resistance, or did she clearly say no. They can ask the more basic question, was there actual consent? Now, does Yes-means-yes mean you need to bring a notary, two witnesses, and a consent form to your date? No. Consent doesn't have to be a signed document. It can be verbal, it can be non-verbal, it can be shown through clear, voluntary participation. The point is not paperwork. The point is that silence, lack of resistance, a previous relationship, or the absence of the word no shouldn't automatically be treated as consent. Hope this clears up the confusion.
